content.title: The Butler Cabin: 5 things you didn’t know about the iconic Augusta National property
content.text: The princess royal has lived there since 1977.The GistGatcombe Park is the home of Princess Anne and her husband Sir Timothy Lawrence.Queen Elizabeth II purchased the property for her only daughter back in 1976.Anne's daughter Zara also lives on the estate with her husband Mike and their three children.Princess Anne's life as Britain's hardest working royal is split between two properties: St. James's Palace and Gatcombe Park. And though the former is arguably more iconic (thanks especially to Prince William and Kate Middleton's 2010 engagement), the latter is where Anne really feels at home."I’ve never been a city girl," the princes royal told The Australian Women’s Weekly in 2020. "I did lessons in London and then because the weekends were at Windsor [Castle] and Windsor has a farm—mostly dairy, but there were pigs and chickens as well—my background in that sense was always on the farm...There was never a question of living in London. It was not a world for me."Nowadays, Anne and her husband Sir Timothy Lawrence manage Gatcombe, which is a working farm, and also share the property with her daughter Zara, her husband Mike, and the couple's three children, all of whom live at Aston Farm, a renovated seven-bedroom farmhouse. Ahead, here's everything you need to know about their life at Gatcombe in Gloucestershire.Gatcombe Park is over 250 years old.Gatcombe Park was built in 1774 and subsequently remodeled in 1820, according to Historic England. Spanning approximately 730 acres, the estate features a main manor house with nine bedrooms, four reception rooms, a library, a billiards room, a conservatory, and a bunch of horse stables (Anne is a lifelong equestrian and became the first member of the royal to compete in the Olympics back in 1976), per Homes & Gardens, The Crown Chronicles and Hello!.The country estate is worth approximately $6 million.Though the price of Gatcombe Park was not disclosed when Queen Elizabeth II purchased it in 1976, the home reportedly cost the late monarch between $500,000 and $750,000, per Homes & Gardens, which, adjusted for inflation, comes to out about $6 million today. That said, operating costs are low given that Gatcombe Park is a working farm, not merely a retreat."It's really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this," Anne once said of the property one the BBC program Countryfile. "Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work. This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise, I can’t stay here."Princess Anne has lived there since 1977.Speaking of Anne, the princess royal has lived at Gatcombe since 1977. Following her mother's purchase of the property in '76 and a year's worth of renovations, she and her then-husband Mark Phillips moved in. (The estate was reportedly a wedding present.) They welcomed their son, Peter Phillips, later that same year and a daughter named Zara four years later, in 1981.In April 1992, Anne and Mark divorced. At that point, both husband and wife had become romantically involved with other people, per Tatler. Anne married her now-husband Timothy Lawrence later that same year; the duo still live at Gatcombe today.It was previously the site of the annual Festival of British Eventing.Aside from its agricultural operations and horse breeding facilities, Gatcombe has played host to several festivals, chief among them the Festival of British Eventing. The annual competition served as a major showcase for elite equestrians and ran from 1983-2023. Event Director Peter Phillips, the princess's son, cited financial concerns when explaining why the festival had become "unfeasible to run."“It is with a heavy heart that The Festival, which has played a significant part in the British Eventing calendar since 1983, cannot run this year," he said in 2024. "The event has also been a huge part of my family’s lives and those of many others for 40 years."His father Mark Phillips, who served as an Event Chairman, added, "It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since Covid, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”Princess Anne's daughter Zara still resides on the estate.Princess Anne's two children lived in cottages at Gatcombe as young adults and eventually moved away after saying "I do." In 2013, however, Zara and her husband Mike Tindall moved back to Gatcombe to raise their children on the estate. The family-of-five now live at Aston Farm, a renovated seven-bedroom farmhouse which was purchased back in 1978."The farmhouse has a rustic yet prominent exterior and a warm and inviting interior which really makes a connection to the great outdoors," interior designer Kunal Trehan told the Daily Express. "Its exterior appears to be a little wild but yet tamed. The interior design is modern but grounded with earthy greys mixed with warm hues and splashes of metallic copper, which echoes the couple’s personality. This is a house that is designed to be lived in, and comfort is at its core."Read the original article on InStyle Princess Anne at Gatcombe Park Festival in August 2025.
